item.title: Sacha Beef
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original recipe with cultural context and technical cooking terms

For anyone who grew up in Taiwan, sacha is a very nostalgic flavor. This condiment is extremely savory (due to dried shrimp and brill fish) and just barely sweet (thanks to shallots and garlic), and is a go-to flavor for stir-fries at Taiwanese beer houses. Sacha beef is probably the most iconic preparation, and when I was developing this dish for 886, I tried skirt steak (too $$$) and flank steak (tough). I wanted something economically feasible with all the fatty goodness of beef. So I took a page from Chinese take-out spots and opted for chuck, which is meaty and delicious but has lots of connective tissue. After a little bit of butchering and then coating the slices of beef in cornstarch and baking soda before stir-frying (a technique called velveting), you get the best of all worlds: a consistently tender, beefy bite. Usually this dish comes with water spinach, but I went with A-choy for sweet freshness, though my craziest addition is butter. It’s not a lot, but it gives the sacha beef an inexplicable depth. Just go with it.

Recipe information

- Total Time 30 minutes (plus 2 hours for marinating)

- Yield 2 servings

Preparation

- Step 1 Marinate the beef: Take 12 oz. (340 g) beef chuck and look for large pieces of muscle, pulling them apart with your hands and slicing away connective tissue to separate each piece. (While you’re at it, trim away any silver skin you see, as it tends to be chewy.) Cut these muscle-y chunks against the grain and into thin slices about 1" by ½" (2.5 by 1.3 cm). Step 2 In a large bowl, combine the beef slices, 1 egg white, whisked until slightly foamy, 1½ tsp. sugar, ¾ tsp. cornstarch, ½ tsp. baking soda, ½ tsp. kosher salt, 2 Tbsp. unsalted Shaoxing rice wine, such as huadiao, or sherry in a pinch, 1 Tbsp. sacha sauce, and 1½ tsp. water. Mix well and store in the fridge for at least 2 hours and up to overnight (12 hours max). Step 3 Now to assemble: Chop 1 large head A-choy (3½ oz. / 100 g) into thirds, roughly 2" (5 cm) long and set aside. Remove the marinated beef from the fridge. Step 4 Heat a wok or heavy-bottomed pan over high heat and drizzle in 1 Tbsp. neutral oil, such as canola. Once the oil is hot and looks loose, slide in the beef. Sauté, stirring every so often, until mostly cooked through and browned all over, about 3 minutes. Remove the beef and set aside. Step 5 Keep the wok over high heat, add ½ white onion, cut into 8 chunks, and cook until slightly translucent, around 1 minute. Pour in 1 Tbsp. sacha sauce (just the paste, not oil on the top) and 1 Tbsp. shallot sauce (just the paste, not oil on top) and throw the beef back in to coat evenly in the sauce. Step 6 Deglaze with ¼ cup (40 g) unsalted Shaoxing rice wine, such as huadiao, or sherry in a pinch and while it’s still steaming, add the A-choy, letting it cook in the residual heat for about 15 seconds. This goes by very quickly, so pay attention to avoid overcooking the A-choy—it should still have structural integrity and not wilt or bend. Step 7 Take the wok off the heat. Stir in ½ tsp. kosher salt, ½ tsp. sugar, and 1½ tsp. unsalted butter until everything is homogeneous. Plate up and serve while still hot.

item.title: Chocolate Mousse With Salty Orange Whip
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: recipe with detailed instructions and cultural background

Chocolate mousse is always a good idea—a classic for a reason. I love to pair the bitterness of chocolate with a lightly sweet and salty cream, but it tastes just as good on its own. Often, I make a double batch, freeze it in quart containers, and let it temper in the fridge the night before I would like to eat it. I serve the mousse with a drizzle of olive oil and fresh raspberries, or I top it with a crunchy brittle. The mousse is also a wonderful cake filling; just be sure to allow it to set fully in the fridge before serving.

Recipe information

- Total Time 30 minutes (plus 2 hours for chilling)

- Yield 8 servings

Ingredients

Chocolate Mousse

Salty Orange Whipped Cream

Toppings (Optional)

Need to make a substitution?

Preparation

- Step 1 To make the chocolate mousse: In a medium saucepan over medium heat, heat 113 g (½ cup) heavy cream until steaming. Remove from the heat and add 170 g (scant 1 cup) coarsely chopped 60% to 70% dark chocolate. Whisk until smooth. Transfer to a medium bowl and let cool to room temperature, about 20 minutes. Step 2 Meanwhile, in the bowl of a stand mixer fitted with the whisk attachment (or in a large bowl with a whisk or handheld mixer), whisk together the remaining 227 g (about 1 cup) heavy cream, 1½ Tbsp. powdered sugar, and ¼ tsp. kosher salt until stiff peaks form, about 4 minutes. Using a rubber spatula, fold a small amount of the whipped cream into the chocolate mixture until combined, then gently fold in the remaining cream, making sure to not beat in too much air. Spoon the mousse into eight serving bowls, cover, and refrigerate for at least 2 hours or up to 4 days. Step 3 To make the salty orange whipped cream: In the bowl of a stand mixer fitted with the whisk attachment (or in a large bowl with a whisk or handheld mixer), whisk together 227 g (1 cup) heavy cream, scant 2 Tbsp. powdered sugar, ½ tsp. kosher salt, 1 tsp. vanilla extract, and 1 tsp. freshly grated orange zest on medium speed until soft peaks form, about 3 minutes. Dollop each chocolate mousse with the salty orange whipped cream. Step 4 If desired, decorate with chocolate shavings or a drizzle of extra-virgin olive oil, fresh raspberries, and a sprinkle of flaky sea salt. Serve immediately.
